title: Which 20 formulas do you need for case interview maths?
description: The twenty formulas case maths keeps using, explained in plain English: profit, margin, break-even, growth, payback and more.
hook: You need twenty formulas for case interview maths: profit, margin, markup, contribution, break-even, payback, ROI, EBITDA, expected value, perpetuity, NPV, CAGR, market share, elasticity, utilisation, LTV, CAC, churn, cost-to-revenue and working capital. None is hard, but you need to know each so well that you never hesitate. Here they are in plain English, with the traps that catch people.
body:
The 20 formulas

TermFormulaWorth knowing
ProfitRevenue − CostsRevenue = volume × price; costs = fixed + variable
Profit marginProfit ÷ RevenueMargin is always on revenue
MarkupProfit ÷ CostMarkup is on cost. See margin vs markup
Contribution marginPrice − Variable cost per unitDrives all break-even maths
Break-even volumeFixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit"How many units to justify it?"
PaybackInvestment ÷ Annual net cash gainCompare with the client's time frame
ROIAnnual profit ÷ InvestmentA yearly rate: compare with the hurdle rate or cost of capital
EBITDARevenue − COGS − Operating costs, before depreciation and amortisationEarnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation; the base for valuation multiples
Expected valueSum of (outcome × probability)Launch, bid and litigation decisions
PerpetuityCash flow ÷ r (growing: CF ÷ (r − g))Value today of a steady stream; in the growing version, CF is next year's cash flow
NPV ruleInvest if NPV > 0Equivalent to the return beating the cost of capital
CAGR(End ÷ Start)^(1 ÷ years) − 1Rule of 72: years to double ≈ 72 ÷ growth %
Market shareOur sales ÷ Market salesSay whether it is units or value
Price elasticity% change in volume ÷ % change in priceState the volume assumption behind any price move
UtilisationActual output ÷ Maximum outputCheck before adding capacity
LTVProfit per customer per year × Years retainedSimple, undiscounted version. Compare with CAC
CACSales and marketing spend ÷ New customersAn LTV:CAC ratio of 3 or more is a common rule of thumb
ChurnCustomers lost ÷ Customers at startRetention = 1 − churn; average lifetime ≈ 1 ÷ churn
Cost-to-revenueEach cost line ÷ Revenue, over timeFinds the cost that is ballooning
Net working capitalInventory + Receivables − PayablesA cash trap in fast-growing businesses

The same list, with a test-yourself mode, is on the formulas page.

Three margins that get confused

"Margin" can mean three different things in conversation, and each answers a different question.

  • Gross margin is (revenue − cost of goods sold) ÷ revenue. It tells you how much the product itself earns.
  • Contribution margin subtracts every variable cost, including things like delivery and payment fees. It tells you what one extra sale adds.
  • Operating margin is operating profit ÷ revenue, after fixed costs and overheads. It tells you how profitable the business is today.

Take a business that charges $100 per order. Product and delivery costs are $55 an order, and payroll and overheads, spread across orders, add another $25. Contribution is $100 − $55 = $45 an order. Operating profit is $45 − $25 = $20 an order.

Use $45 to judge what one more order is worth, because the overheads do not grow with each order. Use $20 to describe how profitable the business is now. Candidates who use $20 for the first question undervalue growth by more than half.

The habit that prevents this: whenever a formula's denominator could be revenue, cost, customers or invested capital, say the denominator out loud.

Three formulas that need extra care

Growing perpetuity

A business will generate $10M next year, growing 3% a year forever, with an 8% discount rate. Value = $10M ÷ (0.08 − 0.03) = $10M ÷ 0.05 = $200M. Without growth it would be $10M ÷ 0.08 = $125M. Two traps: the cash flow must be next year's, not this year's, and the formula only works when growth is below the discount rate.

Churn, lifetime and LTV

A subscription customer brings in $10 of profit a month and monthly churn is 2.5%. Average lifetime is 1 ÷ 0.025 = 40 months, so a simple LTV is 40 × $10 = $400. If acquiring a customer costs $120, LTV:CAC is $400 ÷ $120 = 3.3. Keep the units matched: monthly churn gives a lifetime in months, so multiply by monthly profit. Unit economics shows how to use this in a case.

CAGR

CAGR asks what constant yearly rate would turn the start value into the end value. Revenue going from $50M to $80M in five years is not 60% ÷ 5 = 12% a year. It is 1.6^(1/5) − 1 = 9.9%. Averaging always overstates it. Compound growth and CAGR shows how to estimate it without a calculator.

How to learn them

Cover the middle column of the table and say each formula out loud. Do it once a day for a week and they will stay. Then practise using them in chains, because cases combine them: revenue feeds contribution, contribution feeds break-even, break-even feeds payback.

In the interview, say the formula before the numbers: "Payback is the investment divided by the yearly saving, so $1.2M over $300k: four years." The interviewer can follow your logic, and if you slip on the arithmetic, they can see the method was right.

Practice

1. Revenue grows from $80M to $120M over four years. What is the CAGR, roughly?

Show the answer

End ÷ start is 1.5. 1.1⁴ is 1.46 and 1.11⁴ is 1.52, so the answer sits between: about 10.7% a year. The lazy answer, 50% ÷ 4 = 12.5%, is too high.

2. A machine costs $1.2M and saves $250k a year. What is the payback?

Show the answer

$1.2M ÷ $250k = 4.8 years. Then ask how long the machine lasts: if its life is five years, the investment barely pays back.

3. A retailer holds $30M of inventory, is owed $5M by customers and owes suppliers $20M. What is its net working capital?

Show the answer

$30M + $5M − $20M = $15M. If sales double and these balances grow with them, the retailer needs roughly another $15M of cash, which is why fast growth can strain a profitable business.
